stories.title: How MAGA Inc. raised so much money
stories.text: Trump has made it clear that he has complete authority over the funds, although such direct control is prohibited by law. “This is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control,” Trump said. “I can spend it for what I want to spend it for.” The amount raised by Trump’s super PAC is unprecedented. It is a larger war chest than any entity has ever had to spend in a midterm election. Super PACs supporting former President Joe Biden, for example, raised $57 million in the year after his election . (Biden was also eligible to run again in 2024.) So how is Trump raising so much money? Sarofim is the founder and CEO of Trousdale Ventures, a venture capital firm. (Sarofim previously donated $1 million to Trump’s inaugural committee, according to the New York Times .) Sarofim’s Trousdale Ventures is a major investor in CesiumAstro, which makes communications systems for satellites. Trousdale Ventures has led multiple rounds of financing for the company. CesiumAstro is listed under Sarofim’s “Notable Deals” on his company bio . stories.author: Matt Taibbi
stories.title: Marriage is Wonderful (He Said Controversially)
stories.text: The New York Times just greeted readers with the following headline , as part of a series asking writers to “revisit previously published guest essays”: Eleven years ago, on the occasion of the landmark Obergefell v. Hodges case legalizing gay marriage, the Times asked novelist Elizabeth Curtis Sittenfeld to write a “ Welcome, everyone, to the right to marry !” column. She’s since divorced, so the paper is running her annotated downgrade of the institution. Note the loony image of two ink-blot humanoids crawling off the wedding cake, as if sniffling: We couldn’t do it! It’s too sad! You may or may not find it significant that the Times decided to revisist the merits of marriage at the same time it printed another rethinking-prior-assumptions piece called, “ A Hospital Death Can Be a Good Death .” The last few years have seen a spate of features and columns and TV segments describing “exhaustion” between the sexes. stories.author: Ken Klippenstein
stories.title: The Pentagon’s Million Drone March
stories.text: Pete Hegseth signs memo delivered by drone on Pentagon lawn Fundraising fell off a cliff this summer. Not accepting a dime in corporate ad money allows me to be genuinely independent; but it also means I’m ENTIRELY dependent on readers like you to survive. You read that right. One million . This spending spree is premised on the Pentagon’s frankly dumbass belief that the next war will look like the one Ukraine is fighting (a trench-warfare style slog), rather than the kind the U.S. has spent decades and billions preparing to fight with airpower and long-range precision weapons. Before I explain why that’s (very) wrong, here’s how the military came to that view. As drones shrink in size and AI promises to make them autonomous, the Pentagon is convinced they won't just shape the future of war but usher in a completely new way of waging it. Meanwhile, the Trump administration envisions a Marshall Plan-style program to pump out millions of American-made drones. stories.title: Bankers Rely On Ripping You Off. Wall Street Just Admitted It.
stories.text: A financial magnate just admitted something incredible: If artificial intelligence helps consumers find the best bank interest rates, it may undermine the entire financial system. That suggests the stability of U.S. banks depends on ripping off depositors. New data highlighted by Torsten Slok — a partner and chief economist at the asset management giant Apollo — shows that many fintech apps offer higher deposit interest rates than established banks, potentially ( with a very big asterisk ) giving customers greater returns on their savings. For example, faith-based church and consumer banking app Adelfi offers depositors up to 5 percent interest. stories.author: Drop Site team
stories.title: Washington Is About to Make the Energy Crisis a Whole Lot Worse
stories.text: Eight months into the US-Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz is still contested—and the oil shock nearly everyone predicted never arrived. Gregory Brew, senior energy analyst at Eurasia Group and a historian of modern Iran, explains why crude sits in the $90–$110 band instead of $250: alternative pipeline routes, high global inventories, a steep cut in Chinese imports, and an oil market practiced at absorbing shocks. He also breaks down the US escort operation moving 9 to 10 million barrels a day through the strait—supertankers running dark through the Omani channel—and why he calls it a Band-Aid. Also: the attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, Iranian production down to 2 million barrels a day, record US diesel prices ahead of the midterms, and why Brew expects Tehran to escalate rather than capitulate. stories.title: Trump’s AI Deregulator Has A Billion-Dollar Side Bet
stories.text: As David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s “ AI whisperer ,” urged the White House to take a light-touch approach to AI regulation, the tech tycoon’s venture capital firm launched a new round of investments in AI startups that stood to benefit from the looser rules. Since Sacks left his White House role in March — and concerns have mounted over AI’s potential harms — his firm, Craft Ventures, has continued pumping money into AI startups, including through a gargantuan new $1 billion fund. Sacks was not required to divest from the firm while serving in the Trump administration. Create a FREE account, or log in.
